opening_message:
Ticket 1: Alexandra Johnson (employee ID E003) requests admin access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E003.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Alexandra Johnson (E003) is a full-time Analyst requesting admin access to Source Code. Full-time employees can have up to write, and admin is only allowed if their role owns the system. Source Code is owned by the Engineer role, not Analyst, so admin is not permitted. Granting maximum of write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security record for E003 shows contractor with basic security training, which contradicts the earlier note claiming full-time. Contractors get read at most (write only with advanced training) and never admin. Requested admin exceeds the maximum, so grant read.
reason: E003 (Alexandra Johnson) requested admin access to Source Code. Admin is never permitted here: Source Code is owned by the Engineer role and the employee's role is Analyst, and Source Code is the Engineer-owned system, so even a full-time employee cannot get admin. The security record (verified by database lookup) shows E003 is a contractor with basic security training, which limits access to read (write requires advanced training; admin is never allowed for contractors). The requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum (read), so per policy I grant the maximum allowed level: read.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E003 Alexandra Johnson requests admin access to Source Code.

Two notes:
- Note 1: role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommendation: write. Claims full-time employees can have up to write, admin only if role owns system. Source Code owned by Engineer, so admin not permitted. Grant write max.
- Note 2: role Analyst (not looked up, same as note 1), employment type contractor (looked up), security training basic (looked up), recommendation: read. Contractors get read at most (write only with advanced training), never admin. Requested admin exceeds max, so grant read.

So there's a contradiction: full-time vs contractor. The security agent looked up employment type in their own database before writing and says contractor with basic training. The HR note says full-time but didn't mention how it was verified? Actually note 1 says looked up in own database before writing.

Note 2 says employment type contractor (looked up in own database before writing). Note 2's security record says contractor with basic security training. Also note 2 says security training: basic (looked up).

Hmm. Which to trust? The team memory gives both notes. As the Approver, I need to make a decision based on the evidence available. There's a conflict in employment type. The most cautious/security-oriented approach: contractor with basic training → max read. If full-time → max write (admin not allowed since Analyst doesn't own Source Code). Requested admin > both maximums, so grant the maximum.

Given the conflicting evidence, the safer decision would be read, since the security note indicates contractor with basic training. The security note appears more authoritative for access decisions (security record). The recommendation in note 2 is read.

I'll go with read, citing that admin is not permitted in either case, and based on the security record showing contractor with basic training, max is read.

Actually, let me think: requested admin. If the employee is full-time Analyst, max is write (admin not allowed since role doesn't own system). If contractor with basic training, max is read. Either way, admin is above max, so we grant the maximum. Which maximum? Depends on resolved facts. Security note provides direct database lookup for employment type and security training, both contradicting HR's full-time claim. Since the security agent looked up employment type in their own database and got contractor, and security training basic, max is read.

I'll submit read.
